newsitem.title: KENYA: Refugees are pawns, prize in Great Lakes conflict.
newsitem.headline: Refugees are pawns, prize in Great Lakes conflict.

text.p: Refugees are the pawns and at times the prize in Central Africa's Great Lakes conflict involving Zaire, Rwanda, Burundi and parts of Uganda and Tanzania.
Here are outlines of main groups and how they are linked.
-- The rebel ALLIANCE OF DEMOCRATIC FORCES FOR LIBERATION OF CONGO-ZAIRE has seized much of eastern Zaire, including the towns of Uvira, Kamanyola, Bukavu, Goma and Beni since October.

The revolt, spearheaded by ethnic Tutsi Zaireans who were denied citizenship, uprooted 1.1 million Rwandan and 143,000 Burundian refugees, according to the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

More than 500,000 Rwandan refugees abandoned camps around Goma during fighting between rebel forces and Zairean troops backed by Rwandan Hutu militiamen and former Rwandan troops among the refugees. They fled back into Rwanda in four days from November 15.

The U.S. military estimates 656,500 refugees returned to Rwanda in November and about 60,000 Burundian refugees returned to Burundi. The rest scattered in Zaire and small numbers went to Tanzania and Uganda.
The Rwandan government says most of the refugees in Zaire have returned home.

But U.N. aid agencies say hundreds of thousands are still "missing", some being herded by former troops and militiamen who cannot return to Rwanda because of their role in Rwanda's 1994 genocide which prompted some two million people to flee.

-- The ZAIREAN ARMY, an ill-disciplined force, was pushed back easily by the rebels. Kinshasa has rejected any ceasefire and increased its military budget in a bid to rebuild the armed forces so they can recover what they lost.

-- The 54,000-strong RWANDA PATRIOTIC ARMY is dominated by the country's Tutsi minority, which seized power in July 1994 and ended the genocide launched by the Hutu majority three months earlier. The army backed the rebels in eastern Zaire because it ended attacks by Rwandan Hutu rebels based there.

The U.N. Commission for Human Rights says four Hutu refugees who returned in November were killed after they got back. The RWANDAN GOVERNMENT says returnees suspected of involvement in the genocide will be prosecuted after full investigations.
-- After the return of refugees from Zaire, the TANZANIAN GOVERNMENT, with the cooperation of the UNHCR, set a deadline of December 31 for all 542,000 Rwandan refugees in Tanzania to return home.
The TANZANIAN ARMY and POLICE turned back hundreds of thousands of refugees fleeing away from the Rwandan border last week and has pushed them since Saturday across the border.

-- Zaire accused the UGANDAN ARMY of occupying two Zairean towns. Ugandan officers admit their troops held them for two weeks before withdrawing and handing them over to rebel control. The Ugandan army said they were seized in a hot-pursuit operation over the border against Moslem Ugandan rebels backed by Sudan destabilising southwestern Uganda.

But a link from Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni to Rwandan military strongman Major-General Paul Kagame to the Banyamulenge who fought alongside Kagame's forces in 1994 is at the heart of accusations by Zaire that Rwanda and Uganda back the rebels.
-- The 25,000-strong BURUNDIAN ARMY received a dividend from the Tutsi-led rebellion in Zaire as it uprooted Hutu Burundian rebels based in eastern Zaire and forced them back into Burundi.

Burundi has been under sanctions imposed by regional leaders since shortly after the Tutsi-dominated army seized power in a coup led by Pierre Buyoya on July 25. Its neighbours demand peace talks between the government and Hutu rebels.

The U.N. Commissioner for Human Rights, Jose Ayala Lasso, last week said Burundian troops killed at least 1,100 people in October and November, including hundreds of Hutu refugees forced out of Zaire. Burundi's government denied the army was responsible.
